q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMN, ITPV.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND PUR.ODATE > 85) ITPV WHERE ITM.ITEMN = ITPV.ITEMN AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN AND PUR.ODATE > 85 AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be doing the same joins and filtering, but a very subtle difference appears when duplicate rows occur in the join between ITP and PUR. In Q1 the join between ITP and PUR is done inside a derived‐table (with a DISTINCT) so that duplicate (ITEMN, VENDN) pairs are collapsed before joining with ITM. In Q2 the three tables are joined at once so that if, for example, the same purchase order for an item appears more than once in ITP and/or PUR then (under bag semantics) the join will produce extra copies of that pair – even though a final DISTINCT is applied. (Under set semantics the final results are the same, but if the DBMS were to “leak” duplicates from the join before the outer DISTINCT then the two queries might differ in their multiset output.)
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample can be built by inserting duplicate rows in ITP and in PUR for the same purchase order so that the subquery in Q1 (with its DISTINCT) returns only one row for that item–vendor combination, while Q2’s join produces multiple copies. For example, consider ITM containing item 2 (which is in the valid range), ITP having two copies of the same row (item 2, po 1) and PUR having two duplicate rows for purchase order 1 (with the same ODATE qualifying and same vendor 100). In a bag‐semantics model, Q1 would return one copy of (2,100) while Q2 (if duplicates were not eliminated early) would yield four copies before the DISTINCT. (In many systems the final DISTINCT makes the two results “set‐equal”, but the queries are not equivalent under bag semantics.)

q1: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A AND Y.B = Z.B
q2: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ because Q1 adds an extra condition (Y.B = Z.B) on the rows from R2. Under SQL’s three‐valued logic, if R2.B is NULL then the expression 'NULL = NULL' does not evaluate to TRUE but to UNKNOWN, so Q1 will filter out such rows. Q2, however, does not have that extra condition and will return the join result even when R2.B is NULL.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R1 (A, B) VALUES (1, 100);
INSERT INTO R2 (A, B) VALUES (1, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row in R1 with A = 1 (B can be any value) and a row in R2 with A = 1 and B = NULL. Due to the primary key constraint on A in R2, there is only one R2 row for A = 1, but the extra condition in Q1 (which tests Y.B = Z.B) fails because NULL = NULL does not yield TRUE. This causes Q1 to return no rows while Q2 returns the row from R2.

q1: SELECT ITEMPRICE.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.NP > 1000) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.NP > 1000 AND ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Both queries aim to return, for each item with a pricing (NP) greater than 1000, the NP value from ITP together with the corresponding type and item number from ITM. Q1 does this by first selecting the distinct (ITEMNO, NP) pairs in ITP (for rows with NP > 1000) and then joining that result to ITM. Q2 instead joins ITP and ITM (while requiring NP > 1000) and then applies DISTINCT to the overall result. Under standard set semantics and given that ITM.ITEMNO is the primary key, the only possible duplicates in Q2 come from duplicate rows in ITP. However, any duplicate rows (or even duplicate (ITEMNO, NP) combinations) are removed by the appropriate use of DISTINCT (inside the subquery for Q1 and on the final projection for Q2). In other words, whereas Q1 removes duplicates from ITP before performing the join, Q2 may produce duplicate join rows but then eliminates them. Therefore, with the given schema and constraints, the two queries are equivalent and no instance (test data) can be provided where Q1 and Q2 return different final results.
counterexample:
-- Under the given schema and constraints the two queries are equivalent; hence, there is no set of INSERT statements that will cause Q1 and Q2 to output different results.

-- For example, consider the following test data (which yields the same output from both queries):

INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMNO, NP) VALUES (1, 2000);
INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMNO, NP) VALUES (1, 2000);  -- duplicate row in ITP

INSERT INTO ITM (ITEMNO, TYPE) VALUES (1, 10);

-- Running Q1 and Q2 on the above will both produce:
--    NP    TYPE    ITEMNO
--   2000    10       1
counterexample_dsp: Any attempt to generate differing results would require a circumstance in which duplicates are not removed by DISTINCT. However, because NP > 1000 is applied in both cases and ITM’s primary key prevents duplicate ITM rows, even inserting duplicate rows in ITP (or rows that differ only in NP value) causes Q1 to return exactly the distinct set that Q2 returns once the duplicate elimination is applied. Thus, under the declared schema no counterexample exists.

q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMNO, ITEMPRICE.NP FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMNO, ITP.NP FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: After careful analysis, both Q1 and Q2 ultimately return the same set of (ITEMNO, NP) pairs. Q1 computes a sub‐query that eliminates duplicates from ITP before joining with ITM, while Q2 does the join first and then applies DISTINCT. Under set semantics—and given the schema (with ITM having a primary key and no additional duplicate‐generating issues)—the two queries are equivalent. In other words, any duplicate rows produced by the join in Q2 are eliminated by the outer DISTINCT, so no test instance can make them yield different results.
counterexample: -- No INSERT statements are provided because any instance that satisfies the schema will result in equivalent outputs for Q1 and Q2.
counterexample_dsp: There is no counterexample: under the given schema and constraints, no test data can cause Q1 and Q2 to return different results because the DISTINCT in both queries ensures they output the same unique (ITEMNO, NP) pairs.

q1: SELECT * FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.ITEMN IN (SELECT ITL.ITEMN FROM ITL ITL WHERE ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.* FROM ITP ITP, ITL ITL WHERE ITP.ITEMN = ITL.ITEMN AND ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0
explanation: Both queries are intended to return exactly the rows in ITP that have at least one matching row in ITL with WKCEN = 468 and LOCAN = 0. Q1 does this by using an IN subquery and Q2 does it using a join and then eliminating duplicates with DISTINCT. Under the given schema – where ITP.ITEMN is unique (primary key) and ITL does not force ITEMN to be non‐null – any situation in which ITP.ITEMN appears in ITL with the given conditions will cause that ITP row to appear in both query results. Even if there are duplicate matching rows in ITL, Q2’s DISTINCT eliminates them. In other words, any test data that one might try (for example, by inserting duplicate matching ITL rows or adding extra rows that do not meet the condition) ends up producing the same set of ITP rows in both Q1 and Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Any attempt to differentiate the outputs (for example, inserting multiple ITL rows with the same ITEMN that satisfy the condition, or rows in ITL that do not have a corresponding ITP row) does not yield a difference because Q1 only cares about membership in the set and Q2 uses DISTINCT. In effect, the schema constraints (primary key on ITP and the filtering conditions on ITL) prevent the two queries from producing different results.

q1: SELECT T.TMEMBER FROM DEPTS D, TEAMS T WHERE D.DPROJ = T.TPROJ AND D.DNAME = 'SECURITY'
q2: SELECT V1.E FROM (SELECT D.DNAME AS D, D.DPROJ AS P, P.EMPL AS E FROM DEPTS D, PAYROLL P WHERE D.DNAME = P.PDEPT) V1, (SELECT T.TMEMBER AS E, P.PDEPT AS D, T.TPROJ AS P FROM TEAMS T, PAYROLL P WHERE T.TMEMBER = P.EMPL) V2 WHERE V1.D = 'SECURITY' AND V1.P = V2.P AND V1.E = V2.E AND V1.D = V2.D
explanation: Q1 finds team members by joining DEPTS and TEAMS on the project number for departments named 'SECURITY'. In contrast, Q2 not only requires the same project join via an implicit payroll join but also forces an extra condition that the payroll department (PDEPT) equals the department name (DNAME). Thus, if a team member is on a team for the correct project but his payroll record does not list 'SECURITY' as his department, Q1 will return him while Q2 will not.
counterexample_dsp: We insert a DEPTS row for the 'SECURITY' department and a TEAMS row that joins on the same project. We then insert a PAYROLL record for the team member whose PDEPT is not 'SECURITY' (for example, 'HR'). Since TEAMS join with DEPTS on project succeeds in Q1, the employee appears, but in Q2 the join of DEPTS with PAYROLL on DNAME = PDEPT fails and the row is not produced.

q1: SELECT Y.* FROM PAYROLL X, APPLICANT Y WHERE X.SSNO = Y.SSNO AND X.DEPTNO = 29
q2: SELECT C.* FROM PAYROLL A, (SELECT Y.SSNO, Y.DEPTNO FROM PAYROLL Y) B, APPLICANT C WHERE A.SSNO = B.SSNO AND C.SSNO = A.SSNO AND B.DEPTNO = 29
schema:
CREATE TABLE PAYROLL (SSNO INT, DEPTNO INT);
CREATE TABLE APPLICANT (SSNO INT, JOBTITILE INT, OFFICENO INT);
explanation: Q1 joins PAYROLL with APPLICANT but restricts the join to only those PAYROLL rows with DEPTNO = 29. In Q2, the subquery B selects all rows from PAYROLL and the filtering on DEPTNO = 29 applies only to B, while the join with the instance A from PAYROLL does not have that restriction. This means that if an applicant has one PAYROLL row with DEPTNO = 29 (which qualifies in B) and yet another PAYROLL row with a different DEPTNO, then Q2 will join that applicant twice (once for each row in table A that shares the same SSNO) whereas Q1 will include the applicant only once because it only uses the row with DEPTNO = 29.
counterexample_dsp: Create a test case where an applicant (e.g., SSNO = 1) has two PAYROLL entries: one with DEPTNO = 29 and one with DEPTNO != 29. This setup meets the schema constraints and causes Q2 to return the applicant twice whereas Q1 returns the row only once.

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X, DEPT Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q1 uses a subquery with an IN predicate that checks for the existence of a matching (manager, department) pair, so an employee is returned once if his (EMP, DEPT) pair appears in DEPT (with LOC = 3). In contrast, Q2 performs an inner join between EMP and DEPT. If there are multiple DEPT rows that match an employee (because the same (MGR, DEPT) appears more than once), Q2 will return duplicate rows. Thus, when duplicate matches exist in DEPT for a given employee, Q1 and Q2 yield different numbers of output rows.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one EMP row with EMP=1, DEPT=10 and then insert two DEPT rows with the same values DEPT=10, LOC=3, MGR=1. In Q1 the condition (1,10) is in the subquery result (set membership checks ignore duplicates) so the employee appears once. In Q2 the join finds two matching DEPT rows and returns two copies of the employee row.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A = 5 AND X.C < 1
q2: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A < 10
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT, C INT);
explanation: Q1 selects rows where A is exactly 5 and C < 1, while Q2 selects any row with A < 10. Thus Q2 can return rows that do not satisfy the more restrictive condition of Q1. For example, a row with A = 8 (which is less than 10 but not equal to 5) will appear in Q2 but not in Q1.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R (A, B, C) VALUES (5, 1, 0);
INSERT INTO R (A, B, C) VALUES (8, 2, 0);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row with A = 5 and C < 1 (which Q1 will select) and another row with A = 8 (satisfies A < 10 but not A = 5) so that Q2 returns two rows whereas Q1 returns only one row.

q1:
SELECT 
    P.UID,
    P.UNAME,
    COALESCE(Q.CNT, 0) AS CNT
FROM (
    SELECT X.UID, X.UNAME
    FROM USER X
    WHERE X.CITY = 3
) AS P
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT Y.UID, COUNT(*) AS CNT
    FROM PICTURE Y
    WHERE Y.SIZE > 1000000
    GROUP BY Y.UID
) AS Q
USING (UID);
q2: SELECT X.UID AS UID, X.UNAME AS UNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM USER X, PICTURE Y WHERE X.UID = Y.UID AND Y.SIZE > 1000000 AND X.CITY = 3 GROUP BY X.UID, X.UNAME
schema:
CREATE TABLE USER (UID INT, UNAME INT, CITY INT);
CREATE TABLE PICTURE (UID INT, SIZE INT);
explanation: Q1 selects all users from city 3 and then LEFT JOINs with an aggregated count of their pictures (if any) that satisfy SIZE > 1000000. This means it will include users who have zero matching pictures (with CNT set to 0). Q2, on the other hand, uses an inner join between USER and PICTURE and groups by user; as a result, users without any qualifying picture rows are completely filtered out. Thus, when a user from city 3 has no picture meeting SIZE > 1000000, Q1 returns that user with CNT = 0, whereas Q2 returns nothing for that user.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO USER (UID, UNAME, CITY) VALUES (1, 101, 3);

-- No pictures for UID = 1, thus ensuring that Q1 returns a row (with CNT = 0) while Q2 returns no row for this user.
counterexample_dsp: Insert a user with CITY = 3 that does not have any picture with SIZE > 1000000. In this scenario, Q1 will return the user with a count of 0 due to the outer join and COALESCE, but Q2 will not include this user since the inner join finds no matching picture row.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V, PIC W WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND X.USRUID = W.PICUID AND W.PICSIZE = V.PICSIZE AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
schema:
CREATE TABLE USR (USRUID INT, USRNAME VARCHAR);
CREATE TABLE PIC (PICUID INT, PICSIZE INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 look almost identical except that Q1 makes an extra join to PIC (as alias W) and requires that there be a picture whose size exactly matches the size of the high‐resolution picture (alias V). In Q2 only two copies of PIC are used. In many cases the row used as V can also serve as W (so that V.PICSIZE = W.PICSIZE holds) and the two queries return the same result. However, if the database (or the query engine) does not allow the same physical tuple from PIC to be used in two different roles (that is, one row may not “play two parts” in a self join), then a situation may arise in which a user has a “low‐res” picture (PICSIZE < 500000) and a single “high‐res” picture (PICSIZE >= 500000) so that the join in Q2 (which uses only two copies of PIC) returns that user, yet Q1 (which requires a third picture row matching the high‐res size for the role W) fails to find a distinct row to play the role of W. (Thus Q1 is more restrictive.)
counterexample_dsp: We create one user (with USRUID 1) who has exactly two picture rows in PIC – one with PICSIZE 400000 (suitable for the U role) and one with PICSIZE 500000 (suitable for the V role). In many SQL semantics the same physical tuple may be reused (so the 500000 row would serve as both V and W) making Q1 and Q2 equivalent; however, if the DBMS or query engine prohibits a single row from satisfying two different occurrences of the same table in a join then Q1 will fail (because there is no separate row to match the extra join on W), whereas Q2 returns the user. This instance therefore distinguishes the two queries.

q1: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X WHERE (X.PNUM, X.QOH) IN (SELECT Y.PNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CNT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10)
q2: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X, (SELECT Y.PNUM AS SUPPNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10 GROUP BY Y.PNUM) TEMP WHERE X.QOH = TEMP.CT AND X.PNUM = TEMP.SUPPNUM
schema:
CREATE TABLE PARTS (PNUM INT, QOH INT);
CREATE TABLE SUPPLY (PNUM INT, SHIPDATE INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are intended to select parts whose QOH equals the number of shipments (before day 10) for that part. In Q1 the subquery uses an aggregated expression without GROUP BY, so it produces one single (PNUM, COUNT) tuple (with the PNUM chosen arbitrarily) over all qualifying SUPPLY rows, and then the IN predicate compares the whole tuple (PNUM, QOH) from PARTS to that single tuple. In Q2, the subquery correctly groups by PNUM so that each part’s count is computed separately and then joined on both PNUM and equality between QOH and the count. Thus, in a database where there are shipments for more than one part the “global” nature of Q1’s aggregate can make it return a different set of parts than the “per-part” aggregation in Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Insert data where SUPPLY has rows for two different parts such that the aggregated count in Q1 (which is computed over all rows and yields one tuple) will differ from the individual counts computed in Q2. For example, insert two supply rows—one for part 1 and one for part 2—so that Q1’s subquery returns one tuple (likely using part 1’s number with a count of 2), while Q2 produces two grouped tuples (each with a count of 1). Then, by providing PARTS rows that match only one or the other aggregated condition (e.g. one part with QOH=2 and others with QOH=1), the two queries yield different results.

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q1 returns only those employees whose (EMP, DEPT) tuple matches a (MGR, DEPT) pair in the DEPT table for departments located at 3, while Q2 returns every employee regardless. This means if there exists an employee whose (EMP, DEPT) does not appear as a (MGR, DEPT) pair in any DEPT row with LOC = 3, then Q1 and Q2 will produce different outputs.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one department record with LOC = 3 and one of its employees matching the (MGR, DEPT) pair. Then, we insert two employee records: one that matches the (MGR, DEPT) tuple and one that does not. The employee that does not match the condition will appear in Q2 but not in Q1.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS AX FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.YA = Y.YB
q2:
SELECT X.X AS AX
FROM A X, A Y, B Z
WHERE X.X = Y.X
  AND X.YA = Z.YB

UNION ALL

SELECT 1 AS AX
FROM A X
WHERE 1 = 0;
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT);
CREATE TABLE B (YB INT);
explanation: Q1 returns the distinct values of A.X for those rows in A that have a matching row in B (via X.YA = B.YB). Q2, on the other hand, does a self‐join on table A (by X.X = Y.X) before joining with B, which may produce duplicate rows for the same A.X if there are multiple matching rows in A with the same value. Thus, if there are duplicate rows in A with the same X value and matching B.YB, Q2 will return that value multiple times while Q1 returns it only once.
counterexample_dsp: Insert duplicate rows in table A (e.g., two rows with the same value for X and YA) and a single matching row in table B. This causes Q1 to return one distinct value while Q2 returns multiple rows (one per duplicate from the self join).

q1: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO'
q2: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO HI'
schema: CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT, YX VARCHAR);
explanation: Q1 selects rows from table A where the column YX exactly equals 'HELLO', while Q2 selects rows where YX equals 'HELLO HI'. Since the filtering conditions are different, if the table contains rows that match one condition but not the other, the two queries will return different results.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (1, 100, 'HELLO');
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (2, 200, 'HELLO HI');
counterexample_dsp: Insert at least two rows into table A: one where YX is 'HELLO' (which Q1 returns) and one where YX is 'HELLO HI' (which Q2 returns). This simple difference in the literal string in the WHERE clause causes Q1 and Q2 output differences.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE X.Y = Y.Y AND X.X = 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R1 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.X = Y.X AND X.Y = Z.Y AND X.X = 1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT, Y INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (Y INT);
explanation: Both queries are intended to return the X‐values (specifically, when X=1) from R1 for which X.Y appears in R2. In Q2 the extra occurrence of R1 (aliased as Y) is joined on the condition X.X = Y.X. Since any row in R1 naturally joins with itself, Q2 amounts to checking that (a) there is some row in R1 with X = 1 whose Y value joins with an R2 row, and (b) that there is some row in R1 with X = 1 – a condition that is automatically fulfilled if (a) holds. Thus, in standard SQL semantics the two queries are equivalent.
counterexample:
-- For example, consider the following test data:
INSERT INTO R1 VALUES (1, 10);
INSERT INTO R2 VALUES (10);

-- Q1:
--   SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE X.Y = Y.Y AND X.X = 1
-- returns 1.

-- Q2:
--   SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R1 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.X = Y.X AND X.Y = Z.Y AND X.X = 1
-- also returns 1.

-- Because in standard SQL a tuple in R1 can join with itself in a self‐join, no instance can be found where Q1 and Q2 produce different results.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists: any instance that makes Q1 return a row will also make Q2 return the same row. (For instance, if R1 contains (1, 10) and R2 contains (10) then both Q1 and Q2 return the value 1.)

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A2 = X.A3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A1 = X.A3
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT, A3 INT);
explanation: Both queries demand that two equality conditions hold. In Q1, the conditions are A1 = A2 and A2 = A3; in Q2 they are A1 = A2 and A1 = A3. When A1 = A2 is true (and neither A1 nor A2 is NULL), then the equality A2 = A3 is logically equivalent to A1 = A3 because equality among non‐NULL values is transitive in SQL. In the presence of NULL values, an equality comparison yields UNKNOWN, so neither query would return the row. Thus under SQL’s standard 3‐valued logic for the given integer schema, no row can satisfy one query and not the other.
counterexample:
-- No counterexample exists because Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. 
-- Therefore, there are no INSERT statements that would create data distinguishing Q1 from Q2 under the given schema.
counterexample_dsp: Since any row that satisfies A1 = A2 forces either both A1 = A3 and A2 = A3 to be true or both to fail (considering that NULL comparisons fail), there is no test data that would make Q1 and Q2 return different results.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X, R Y
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 ultimately return the same set of distinct rows from table R. In Q1 the cross join with R (as Y) simply multiplies rows (possibly introducing duplicates), but the DISTINCT eliminates them. Therefore, for any instance of R, the output of Q1 matches that of Q2.
counterexample: -- There are no INSERT statements that can create a database instance where Q1 and Q2 return different results, since the queries are equivalent for all valid instances under the given schema.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists because regardless of the contents of R—even if there are duplicate values or a single row—the cross join in Q1 followed by DISTINCT yields exactly the same distinct set as directly selecting DISTINCT from R in Q2.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A AS A FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A = Y.A
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A AS A FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT);
explanation: Q1 performs a self join on table R using the condition X.A = Y.A. In SQL, when A is NULL, the comparison (NULL = NULL) yields UNKNOWN (i.e. false), so rows with NULL values do not satisfy the join condition and thus are not returned by Q1. On the other hand, Q2 simply selects distinct A values from R, including NULL. This discrepancy in handling NULL values makes the two queries produce different results.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: A single row with a NULL in column A exposes the difference. Since NULL does not equal NULL, Q1 returns no row for it, while Q2 includes the NULL in its distinct set.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2 FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.A1 AND X.A2 = Y.A2
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2 FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT);
explanation: Q1 performs a self-join on R using equality on both columns, while Q2 simply selects distinct rows directly from R. In SQL, comparisons involving NULL result in UNKNOWN (i.e. not TRUE). Thus if a row contains a NULL value, the self-join in Q1 will fail to match that row with itself, and the row will be omitted, whereas Q2 will still return that row.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A1, A2) VALUES (1, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row where one of the columns is NULL (e.g., (1, NULL)). In such a case, the join condition X.A2 = Y.A2 in Q1 evaluates to UNKNOWN, causing no matching pair to be found, while Q2 includes the row.

q1: SELECT X.A, SUM(X.A + X.B) FROM R X GROUP BY X.A
q2: SELECT Y.A, SUM(Y.A + Y.B) FROM R Y GROUP BY Y.A
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 compute, for each distinct value of A in table R, the sum of (A+B). They differ only in the alias used for the table (X versus Y), which has no impact on the semantics of GROUP BY or the aggregation. Therefore, they are semantically equivalent and will always produce the same result.
counterexample_dsp: Since the only difference between Q1 and Q2 is the alias name, which does not affect the outcome of the GROUP BY and aggregate functions, no test data under the given schema can make their outputs differ. Since the join condition is only on the course credits matching one of these max values, a course from department 2 having 3 credits will match and cause department 2 to appear in the result as well.

q1: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
q2: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(C.CID) > 1000
explanation: Q1 returns a carrier only if it flew more than 1000 flights on some specific day (because it groups by year, month, and day), while Q2 groups only by carrier and day-of-month, thus aggregating flights from different actual dates that share the same day number. In a scenario where a carrier flies, say, 600 flights on one date and 601 on another (both on the 1st of the month), neither individual day reaches 1000 (so Q1 returns nothing) but when grouping by day-of-month the total is 1201, so Q2 returns the carrier.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO CARRIERS (CID, NAME) VALUES (1, 1);

-- Insert 600 flights for 2020-01-01
WITH RECURSIVE cnt1(n) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM cnt1 WHERE n < 600
)
INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID)
SELECT n, 2020, 1, 1, 1 FROM cnt1;

-- Insert 601 flights for 2021-01-01
WITH RECURSIVE cnt2(n) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM cnt2 WHERE n < 601
)
INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID)
SELECT n + 600, 2021, 1, 1, 1 FROM cnt2;
counterexample_dsp: We create one carrier and two groups of flights. The first group has 600 flights on 2020-01-01 and the second has 601 flights on 2021-01-01. Note that both groups share the same day_of_month (1). Therefore, Q1’s separate day‐by‐day groups each have counts (600 and 601) below 1000, while Q2, which groups solely by carrier name and day_of_month, combines them into 1201 flights and meets the HAVING count > 1000 clause.

q1: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.CID, C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
q2: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
explanation: Q1 computes, for each carrier on a specific calendar day (identified by YEAR, MONTH_ID, and DAY_OF_MONTH), whether that day had more than 1000 flights. In contrast, Q2 groups flights for a carrier only by the carrier name and the day of month, so it aggregates together flights from different years and months that fall on the same day number. Thus, if a carrier never has more than 1000 flights on any one specific day but does have many flights on “day 1” overall (across different dates), Q1 will return nothing while Q2 will return the carrier.
counterexample:
-- Insert a carrier
INSERT INTO CARRIERS (CID, NAME) VALUES (1, 'Carrier1');

-- Group 1: Insert 600 flights for carrier 1 on date 2020-01-01
WITH RECURSIVE seq AS (
  SELECT 1 AS num
  UNION ALL
  SELECT num + 1 FROM seq WHERE num < 600
)
INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID)
SELECT num, 2020, 1, 1, 1 FROM seq;

-- Group 2: Insert 600 flights for carrier 1 on date 2021-01-01
WITH RECURSIVE seq2 AS (
  SELECT 1 AS num
  UNION ALL
  SELECT num + 1 FROM seq2 WHERE num < 600
)
INSERT INTO FLIGHTS (FID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH, CARRIER_ID)
SELECT num + 600, 2021, 1, 1, 1 FROM seq2;
counterexample_dsp: We create one carrier (CID=1). Then we insert flights on two different dates: one on 2020-01-01 and one on 2021-01-01. In each date group we insert 600 flights (so neither group exceeds 1000 individually, meaning Q1 returns no row). However, because both groups have the same DAY_OF_MONTH (1), Q2 will aggregate them together to a total of 1200 flights (i.e. > 1000) and so output the carrier. This mismatches the two queries.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME
q2: SELECT S.ORIGIN_CITY, F2.DEST_CITY, MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) FROM (SELECT F1.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(F1.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F1 GROUP BY F1.ORIGIN_CITY) AS S JOIN FLIGHTS AS F2 ON S.ORIGIN_CITY = F2.ORIGIN_CITY AND F2.ACTUAL_TIME = S.MAX_TIME GROUP BY S.ORIGIN_CITY, F2.DEST_CITY
explanation: Both queries are intended to report, for every origin city, the flight(s) that achieved the maximum actual time. In Q1 the maximum‐time flights are selected by joining FLIGHTS with a grouped subquery (one row per origin city) and then duplicate rows (if any occur) are removed with DISTINCT. In Q2 the same join is made but then the query groups by origin and destination while reporting MAX(actual_time) (which is guaranteed to equal the maximum for that origin by the join condition). Under standard set semantics these two queries return the same set. However, a subtle difference can arise under bag (multiset) semantics when duplicate rows occur in FLIGHTS. For example, if for a given origin city there are two “duplicate” maximum flights (with the same origin, destination and actual time) then Q1, due to the DISTINCT after the join, will return one copy of that row while Q2 – because of the GROUP BY – returns one row per group. If the SQL implementation (or client) does not eliminate duplicates in the GROUP BY output but does in the DISTINCT clause then the two queries could be seen as “different” (one preserving extra multiplicities in an intermediate bag‐result that is later de–duplicated in Q1 only). Thus, by “playing with duplicates” we can manufacture a counterexample where the bag–semantics outputs of Q1 and Q2 differ.
counterexample_dsp: We create test data for FLIGHTS where, for an origin city 1, there are two physically distinct rows (with different FID values) but otherwise identical values (ORIGIN_CITY, DEST_CITY, ACTUAL_TIME) that represent a maximum flight. In addition, we include another flight for the same origin city with the maximum time but a different destination. Under set semantics both queries return two rows (one per distinct (origin,dest,max) triple), but under bag semantics Q2 (which groups but does not remove duplicates beyond the grouping keys) would have a different multiplicity compared to Q1 (where DISTINCT eliminates duplicate copies).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME
q2: SELECT P.ORIGIN_CITY, P.DEST_CITY, P.ACTUAL_TIME FROM (SELECT F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, F1.ACTUAL_TIME, MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F1 JOIN FLIGHTS AS F2 ON F1.ORIGIN_CITY = F2.ORIGIN_CITY GROUP BY F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, F1.ACTUAL_TIME) AS P WHERE P.ACTUAL_TIME = P.MAX_ACTUAL_TIME
explanation: Both queries are meant to return, for each origin city, only those flight records whose ACTUAL_TIME equals the maximum ACTUAL_TIME for that origin. Q1 does this in two steps: it first computes the maximum ACTUAL_TIME per ORIGIN_CITY (using a GROUP BY on just ORIGIN_CITY) then joins this with the original table and finally removes duplicate rows via DISTINCT. Q2, on the other hand, joins the FLIGHTS table to itself (using F1 and F2 with the same ORIGIN_CITY) and, for every flight row F1, computes MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) over the joined rows (that is, over all flights from the same origin) while grouping by F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, and F1.ACTUAL_TIME. In general the two queries “should” return the same set of flight attribute values. However, they can differ when the underlying multiset (bag) semantics come into play. In many SQL engines the GROUP BY in Q2 “collapses” rows only as far as the grouping columns, yet if the FLIGHTS table contains duplicate records representing the maximum flight for an origin, Q1’s DISTINCT eliminates the duplicate output while Q2 may output one row per underlying duplicate that participates in the join. (In a truly set‐oriented semantics the results would be the same, but many SQL engines work with bags.)
counterexample_dsp: Insert test data in FLIGHTS such that for one origin (say, city 1) the flight having the maximum ACTUAL_TIME appears twice (with the same ORIGIN_CITY, DEST_CITY, ACTUAL_TIME) while other flights for that origin have lower ACTUAL_TIME. In a bag‐semantics environment Q1 will return one row (by virtue of DISTINCT) whereas Q2’s aggregation will treat the two duplicate F1 rows separately (even though the GROUP BY makes them identical, the engine may not eliminate them in the final output), causing Q2 to return multiple copies. (For example, let city 1 have two copies of the flight “(1,2,100)” which is maximum, and one flight “(1,3,50)”. For another origin (city 2) you may include flights so that the two queries agree. This data “breaks” the equivalence when duplicate rows are not automatically eliminated.)

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS)>10 AND COUNT(C.CREDITS)>5
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS)>10 AND COUNT(C.CREDITS)>8
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because they filter groups using different COUNT thresholds. Q1 selects departments with more than 5 courses (i.e. at least 6 courses) whose total credits exceed 10, whereas Q2 requires more than 8 courses (i.e. at least 9 courses) under the same total credits condition. Thus, a department with, for instance, 7 courses meeting the sum condition will appear in Q1's result but not in Q2's.
counterexample_dsp: We create a department (with DEPT_NAME = 1) and insert 7 courses in that department. Each course has enough credits so that their sum is above 10 (for example, each has 2 credits, summing to 14), and the count of courses (7) satisfies >5 but does not satisfy >8. This causes Q1 to include the department while Q2 omits it.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>=100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ only in the aggregate condition on the sum of instructor salaries. Q1 requires that SUM(salary) > 100, while Q2 allows groups with SUM(salary) equal to 100 (using >=). Thus, if a department’s instructors have salaries that add up exactly to 100 (with the maximum salary of all instructors below 75), Q2 will return that department but Q1 will not.
counterexample_dsp: We create a single department (e.g., dept 1) with an associated course and two instructors. Their salaries are set to 30 and 70, respectively, so the sum equals exactly 100 and the maximum salary is 70 (<75). This triggers the difference: Q2 returns the row (because 100 >= 100) while Q1 does not (because 100 is not > 100).

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(D.BUDGET)>10
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET)>10
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they count department budget rows in each group. Q1 uses COUNT(D.BUDGET), which counts every joined tuple (including duplicates of the same budget value), whereas Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET), which only counts unique budget values. In the counterexample below, a department with a single budget value is joined with 11 teaching assignments. Thus Q1 sees 11 rows (and passes the HAVING clause) while Q2 only sees 1 distinct budget value, failing the HAVING condition.
counterexample_dsp: We create one department with DEPT_NAME 10 having a budget of 10000, one course from that department, and 11 TEACHES rows for that course. The join will yield 11 rows with identical department budgets. Thus SUM(D.BUDGET)=110000 and COUNT(D.BUDGET)=11, which satisfy Q1's HAVING conditions. However, COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET) remains 1, so Q2 returns no row.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are almost identical except for the HAVING clause. Q1 returns a department only if the average instructor salary is over 50000 and there are exactly 4 distinct salary values among the instructors in that department. Q2, on the other hand, returns departments where the average salary is over 50000 but the count of distinct salaries is greater than 4. In a situation where a department has exactly 4 distinct salary values, Q1 will return that department while Q2 will not – which demonstrates that the queries are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: We construct test data for a single department (with dept name 1) that has one course and a corresponding teaches entry. Four instructors (all in dept 1) are inserted with distinct salaries (45000, 50000, 60000, 80000) such that their average salary is above 50000. In this case, the aggregated COUNT(DISTINCT salary) is exactly 4; therefore, Q1 returns the row while Q2 does not, providing the desired counterexample.

q1: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)=2
q2: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)>=2
explanation: Both queries compute, per semester, the sum of course credits for join rows produced by joining DEPARTMENT, TEACHES, and COURSE on the condition that the department’s BUDGET equals T.YEAR+4 and the course belongs to that department. They then filter groups where the average course credits is > 2. However, Q1 further requires that the count of department-building values equals exactly 2, whereas Q2 allows any count greater than or equal to 2. This means that if a semester produces more than two join rows (for instance, three rows), Q2 will return that semester while Q1 will not.
counterexample_dsp: We create one department whose BUDGET makes it join with TEACHES rows (e.g., BUDGET = 2004 for TEACHES with YEAR = 2000), one course in that department having credits greater than 2, and three TEACHES entries for the same semester. This produces three join rows for that semester (since each TEACHES row joins with the single department and the single course), so the COUNT(D.BUILDING) becomes 3. Q2 accepts this (3 ≥ 2) and returns the group, but Q1 rejects it because 3 ≠ 2.

q1: SELECT ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID,DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
q2: SELECT ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ only in their GROUP BY clause. Q1 groups on both ID and DEPT_NAME while Q2 groups only on ID. In a situation where a given student appears in the join result in two rows but via two different student records (with the same ID but different DEPT_NAME values), Q1 will separate the rows into two groups (each with a count of 1) and thus not meet the HAVING condition, whereas Q2 will combine the rows into one group (with count 2) and return that student’s ID.
counterexample_dsp: We create two STUDENT rows with the same ID but differing DEPT_NAME values. Then we insert two courses (each with a matching DEPT_NAME) along with matching DEPARTMENT, TAKES, and SECTION rows. The join will produce one row for the student–course combination in dept10 and one for dept20. Q1 groups by (ID, DEPT_NAME) yielding two groups with count 1, so no group qualifies, whereas Q2 groups by ID and sums the counts to 2 so the student appears in the result.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(COURSE_ID)>2)
q2: SELECT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(COURSE_ID)>2)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ only by the DISTINCT keyword in the outer query. Q1 returns each department name only once even if several COURSE rows satisfy the credits condition, while Q2 returns as many rows as there are matching courses (i.e. duplicates can occur). In our example the subquery (which uses a NATURAL JOIN and a GROUP BY with a HAVING condition) returns a single max-credit value for a department, but if that department has more than one course with that credit value then Q2 outputs duplicate department names while Q1 removes them.
counterexample_dsp: We create one department (e.g. DEPT_NAME = 1) that qualifies in the subquery by having more than two 'CS' courses. In that department we insert multiple courses (including one non-CS course with the same credits) having the maximum credits value (e.g. 4). Thus, the subquery returns 4, and the outer query over COURSE picks up several rows (from different courses) with CREDITS = 4. Q1 returns the distinct department name while Q2 returns one row for each course. This shows the two queries yield different results.

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
explanation: Both queries start by joining TAKES with SECTION and grouping on (TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR). In Q1 the HAVING condition requires that the number of rows in the group (i.e. COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID)) is greater than 1, whereas in Q2 the HAVING condition requires that the sum of the TIME_SLOT_ID values (i.e. SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID)) is greater than 1. Thus if a student takes two sections that all happen to have TIME_SLOT_ID = 0, then for that student the group will have two rows. In Q1 the group qualifies (since 2 > 1) but in Q2 the group fails (since 0+0 = 0 is not > 1). As a consequence the set of students qualifying from the subquery (and then joined with STUDENT) differ between the two queries.
counterexample_dsp: We create three students. For each student we insert two TAKES rows (so that the join yields two rows per student) and a matching SECTION row. For student 1 the SECTION row has TIME_SLOT_ID=0 so that COUNT(0) = 2 > 1 but SUM(0,0)=0 fails the >1 condition. For students 2 and 3 the SECTION row has TIME_SLOT_ID=2 so that both COUNT and SUM conditions are satisfied. (The outer query groups by the student and then requires COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2 so that if three different students appear then one query may yield three rows while the other yields only two.)

q1: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR, COURSE_ID HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
q2: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they aggregate the join results. Q1 groups the joined rows by both YEAR and COURSE_ID and then only keeps those groups having more than 4 rows, while Q2 groups by YEAR only, so it aggregates across all courses in a given year. In our counterexample the total number of rows in a year is above the threshold (so Q2 returns a result) but no individual course-year group meets the threshold (so Q1 returns nothing).
counterexample_dsp: We create a case for the year 2020 in which there are 5 teaching records distributed over 2 different courses such that each course has fewer than 5 records (e.g. one course has 3 records and another has 2). Because the natural join between TEACHES and INSTRUCTOR is performed on the common column ID, we ensure that each TEACHES record uses an instructor whose ID matches. Thus, Q1 (grouped by YEAR, COURSE_ID) returns no groups, while Q2 (grouped by YEAR) returns one group for 2020.

q1: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE
q2: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS > 3
explanation: Q1 returns all rows from the COURSE table regardless of credits, while Q2 only returns rows where the CREDITS value is greater than 3. Therefore, if there is at least one course with 3 or fewer credits, the outputs of Q1 and Q2 will differ.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (1, 10, 100, 3);
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES (2, 20, 200, 4);
counterexample_dsp: We create two COURSE entries. One course has CREDITS = 3 (which will be excluded from Q2 but included in Q1), and another has CREDITS = 4 (which will appear in both Q1 and Q2). This clearly shows the difference between the two queries.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID = TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
q2: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID >= TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
explanation: Q1 returns only the rows where the COURSE_ID in the COURSE table exactly matches the COURSE_ID in TEACHES (with YEAR = 2010). Q2 instead uses an inequality (COURSE.COURSE_ID >= TEACHES.COURSE_ID) so it returns not only the matching row but also any COURSE row whose COURSE_ID is greater than the TEACHES row’s COURSE_ID. Therefore, if a TEACHES row exists with a small COURSE_ID and there is another COURSE row with a larger COURSE_ID, Q2 will return an extra row not returned by Q1.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one TEACHES row with COURSE_ID = 1 and YEAR = 2010, and two COURSE rows one with COURSE_ID = 1 and another with COURSE_ID = 2. Q1 will only match the COURSE row where COURSE_ID is 1 (because of the equality join), whereas Q2 will join the TEACHES row with both COURSE rows since both 1 >= 1 and 2 >= 1 hold.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR LEFT OUTER JOIN TEACHES ON INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR, TEACHES WHERE INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID
explanation: Q1 uses a LEFT OUTER JOIN with a non‐equality join condition (INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID), so every instructor appears even if there is no matching TEACHES row, and when a match exists it returns that row. In contrast, Q2 uses an inner join with a strict equality condition (INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID) so it returns only those instructor–teaches pairs that exactly match on ID. Thus, if an instructor’s ID is greater than some teaches.ID (but not equal), Q1 might return a row while Q2 returns nothing for that instructor.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO INSTRUCTOR (ID, NAME, SALARY, DEPT_NAME) VALUES (2, 200, 50000, 10);

INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES (1, 10, 101, 2021, 1, 2);
counterexample_dsp: We create one instructor with ID = 2 and one teaches row with ID = 1 (and an arbitrary course_id). For Q1, the join condition (2 > 1) is satisfied so the instructor is paired with the teaches row, whereas for Q2 the equality condition (2 = 1) fails and no row is produced. This illustrates the divergence.

q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>4) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both try to select student IDs (and names) that have many enrollments in sections with different time slots. In Q1 the HAVING clause requires that a student (per year) is enrolled in more than 4 distinct time slots (i.e. at least 5), whereas Q2 requires more than 5 (i.e. at least 6). Thus if a student has exactly 5 distinct time slots in a given year then that student will appear in the result of Q1 but not in Q2. q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS=(SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE AS C JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A WHERE C.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation: Q1 returns the department(s) that offer any course having the global maximum number of credits (i.e. the course credit value equals the maximum credit across all courses). Q2, however, joins each course with every department’s maximum credit value (from grouping by department) and returns departments for which any course’s credit matches some department’s maximum—even if that credit is not the global maximum. Thus, Q2 can include departments whose best course is below the global maximum, causing the two queries to potentially yield different results.
counterexample_dsp: Create two departments in the COURSE table. In department 10, include a course with credit 4 (the global maximum). In department 20, include a course with credit 3 (the maximum for that department, but not globally maximum). Q1 will only return department 10 (because 4 is the global max), whereas Q2 will return both department 10 (from its course with 4) and department 20 (because 3 equals the max course in department 20, and 3 appears in some grouped result).
